title: Quantifying Symmetry Breaking
abstract: Quantifying properties of quantum states through the limits of their manipulation is a central goal of quantum resource theories. For symmetry breaking, the quantum geometric tensor governs asymptotic pure-state conversion, but a complete characterization for general mixed states has remained elusive.   Here we fully resolve this problem for finite-dimensional systems under compact Lie group symmetries in the i.i.d. asymptotic regime. Specifically, we establish a single-letter formula for the optimal conversion rate between arbitrary states, with vanishing trace-distance error, in the resource theory of asymmetry. The rate is determined by a one-parameter family of quantum Fisher information (QFI) matrices that interpolates between the symmetric- and right-logarithmic-derivative QFIs. No state-independent finite subset of this family suffices in general, even for $U(1)$ symmetry, revealing a qualitative distinction from pure-state conversion. Our formula further yields an exact formula for pure-state distillation rates in terms of the generalized quantum geometric tensor, characterizes asymptotically reversible interconversion, and identifies bound asymmetry for quantum clocks. Complementarity among different members of the QFI family also uncovers an activation mechanism for quantum clocks.   Our proof relies on two developments of independent interest. First, we extend quantum local asymptotic normality to unitary models with arbitrary rank and spectral degeneracy. Second, we characterize convertibility between quantum Gaussian shift models in terms of the same one-parameter family of QFIs. Together, these results provide an operational characterization of symmetry breaking for general quantum states in the i.i.d. asymptotic regime and reveal how distinct QFI constraints give rise to irreversibility and activation.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive resource theory approach to quantify symmetry breaking in mixed quantum states. It establishes that the optimal conversion rate is governed not by a single measure, but by an entire continuous family of Quantum Fisher Information matrices. This reveals a fundamental difference between pure-state and mixed-state resource quantification.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a complete, operational characterization for quantifying symmetry breaking in general mixed quantum states within the i.i.d. asymptotic limit.
main_result: It establishes a single-letter formula for the optimal conversion rate between arbitrary mixed states, determined by an entire one-parameter family of Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrices.
method: The analysis uses quantum resource theories, extending quantum local asymptotic normality (QLAN) to complex unitary models and characterizing convertibility via the continuous QFI family.
model_or_system: The study concerns quantum systems in finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces subjected to compact Lie group symmetries, analyzing the conversion of many copies of input states ($ho^{\otimes n}$) to output states ($ho'^{\otimes m}$).
key_observables: Asymmetry measure, Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrices (interpolating SLD and RLD), and the generalized quantum geometric tensor (QGT).
important_parameters: The asymptotic regime (i.i.d.), the parameter $q$ defining the QFI family, and the group structure of the symmetry $G$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the i.i.d. asymptotic regime, and the proof relies on extending QLAN to arbitrary rank unitary models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes the findings, contrasting the single-measure characterization for pure-state conversion (using QGT) with the full QFI family required for general mixed-state conversion.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general problem of resource quantification, develops the necessary mathematical tools (like extended QLAN), derives the single-letter formula using the continuous QFI family, and then specializes the results to pure-state distillation and asymmetry activation.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for understanding how symmetry constraints dictate the fundamental limits of quantum information processing, which has implications for characterizing non-equilibrium processes in many-body systems.
